title: Hair Care & Simple Styling

modules.title: Understanding Afro-Textured Hair, Moisture and a Safe Workstation
modules.overview: Before you braid a single row, you need to understand why afro-textured hair is beautiful but fragile, how it loses and keeps moisture, and how to set up tools that will not spread infection. This module gives you that foundation, with a simple wash-day routine and a hygiene system you will use for every client.

lessons.title: How afro-textured hair grows, and why it breaks
objectives: Describe the three layers of a hair strand and what each one does
Identify curl patterns from 3 to 4C and porosity levels in real heads of hair
Explain why tightly coiled hair is often dry and breaks easily
Recognise healthy scalp signs and the warning signs that need a doctor

blocks.text: Most women in this course will work on **afro-textured hair**: hair that grows in tight coils, zig-zags and spirals. It is the most common hair type in Nigeria and across Africa. It is not "hard" or "bad" hair. It simply has a shape that needs a particular kind of care. Once you understand the shape, many everyday problems like breakage, dryness and thin edges start to make sense.

blocks.name: woman-emoji-component-curly-hair
blocks.alt: A woman with full curly hair
blocks.caption: Coily hair is strong in volume but fragile at every bend, which is why gentle handling matters.

blocks.text: What a single strand is made of

Each hair grows from a **follicle**, a small pocket in the skin of the scalp. The part you can see is dead protein called **keratin**, so hair cannot heal itself once it is damaged. A strand has three layers:

items: **Cuticle**: the outer layer of flat, overlapping scales, like roof tiles. When the scales lie flat, hair looks shiny and holds water. When they are lifted or broken, hair feels rough and loses moisture fast.
**Cortex**: the thick middle layer that gives hair its strength, elasticity and colour. Relaxers and bleach work by changing the cortex, which is why they can weaken hair.
**Medulla**: a soft core found in some thicker hairs. It does not matter much for everyday care.

blocks.text: The scalp also makes a natural oil called **sebum**. On straight hair, sebum slides down the strand easily. On tightly coiled hair, it struggles to travel past each bend, so the ends stay dry even when the scalp feels oily. This is one main reason afro-textured hair needs regular moisture from outside.
Why coils break

Every bend in a coil is a weak point. When hair is combed dry, pulled tight or brushed hard, the strand snaps at those bends. Coils also wrap around each other and form knots, especially at the ends. That is why gentle detangling, moisture and low tension are the three rules you will hear again and again in this course.
Curl pattern and porosity

Many stylists use a simple typing chart made popular by the hairstylist Andre Walker: type 1 is straight, type 2 wavy, type 3 curly and type 4 coily. Type 4 is split into 4A (springy S-shaped coils), 4B (sharper Z-shaped bends) and 4C (very tight coils that shrink a lot). One head can have two or three patterns, often tighter at the nape and looser at the crown. Use the chart as a quick language with clients, not as a strict rule.

head: Porosity
What it means
What you notice
What helps
rows: Water beads on the hair, products sit on top, hair takes long to dry
Light products, warm water or a warm towel to help moisture in
Hair takes in water and holds it fairly well
A regular routine is usually enough
Cuticle is raised or damaged, often after relaxers, colour or heat
Hair soaks up water quickly but dries out fast, feels rough
Leave-in conditioner, sealing with oil or butter, less heat

blocks.text: **Porosity** describes how easily water gets into the hair and stays there. The popular "float test" (dropping a strand into a cup of water) is not reliable, because products and oils on the hair change the result. A better check is to watch how hair behaves on wash day: how fast it gets wet, how long it takes to dry, and how quickly it feels dry again after moisturising.
Hair grows in a cycle

Each follicle goes through a growing phase that lasts years, a short resting phase, and then the old hair sheds so a new one can grow. Losing some hairs every day is normal. When a client takes down braids after six weeks, she will see a ball of shed hair, because the hairs that shed during those weeks were trapped in the braids. Explain this calmly so she does not panic.

blocks.title: The hair growth cycle
items: Growing phase (years)
Short transition phase
Resting phase
Old hair sheds
New hair grows
blocks.caption: Shedding is part of a normal cycle; breakage is different and usually comes from handling.

blocks.title: Worked example: shedding or breakage?
blocks.context: For example, Amaka in Onitsha takes down her client Blessing's braids after seven weeks. Blessing is worried by the hair in the comb.
steps: Amaka picks up a few loose hairs and looks at one end of each. Shed hairs have a tiny white bulb at the root end.
Most hairs have the bulb, so they are shed hairs. A few short pieces with no bulb are broken pieces.
She notices most broken pieces came from the nape, where the braids were smallest and the hair was driest.
She advises a deep conditioning treatment, a looser and slightly bigger braid at the nape next time, and nightly moisture there.
blocks.result: Blessing understands the difference between normal shedding and breakage, and Amaka has a clear change to make on the next style.

blocks.title: When to refer to a doctor
blocks.text: Do not style over scaly round patches with broken hairs, pus, open sores, bleeding, or bald patches with no clear cause. Tell the client kindly and suggest a clinic or dermatologist. Scaly patches with broken hairs, especially in children, can be ringworm of the scalp, which spreads through combs and towels.

takeaways: Hair is dead keratin, so damage cannot heal; prevention is everything
Coily hair is dry because sebum cannot travel down the bends
Breakage happens at the bends, so moisture, gentle detangling and low tension matter
Daily shedding is normal; broken pieces without a bulb mean damage
Never style over signs of infection; refer kindly

activity.title: Read three heads of hair
steps: Ask three people (yourself, a relative and a friend) if you may look at and touch their hair.
For each person, note the curl pattern at the front, crown and nape.
Wet a small section with a spray bottle and note how fast it absorbs water and how fast it dries.
Look at the scalp for flakes, redness, bumps or thin areas, and write what you see.
Write one sentence of care advice for each person.
activity.evidence: A short note or table for the three people with curl pattern, porosity guess, scalp notes and advice.

lessons.title: Wash day: cleansing, conditioning and the LOC method
objectives: Plan a wash-day routine for natural or relaxed hair
Detangle hair safely from ends to roots
Apply the LOC or LCO method to keep hair moisturised
Choose products by reading labels instead of brand promises

blocks.text: Clean, moisturised hair is easier to style, breaks less and gives neater braids. A good wash day is the foundation of every service you will sell. Many stylists and dermatologists suggest washing afro-textured hair about once every one to two weeks, adjusting for sweat, dandruff and the style being worn. Washing every day strips the little sebum the hair has.

blocks.name: lotion-bottle
blocks.alt: A pump bottle of hair lotion
blocks.caption: Water moisturises; creams and oils help keep that water in the hair.

blocks.text: The wash-day order

items: **Pre-poo (optional)**: apply oil or conditioner to dry hair for 15 to 30 minutes before washing to reduce tangles and protect the ends.
**Section**: divide the hair into four to six sections with clips or loose twists. Working in sections prevents matting.

**Shampoo the scalp**: focus shampoo on the scalp with the pads of your fingers, not your nails. Let the lather run down the length. A sulphate-free shampoo is gentler for regular use; a clarifying shampoo removes build-up but is drying, so use it occasionally.
**Condition**: apply conditioner to the length and ends. Leave it on for the time on the label.
**Detangle while conditioner is in**: use fingers first, then a wide-tooth comb, starting at the ends and working up to the roots.
**Rinse with cool or lukewarm water**, then blot with a cotton T-shirt or microfibre towel instead of rubbing.
**Moisturise and seal** with the LOC or LCO method, then stretch the hair in twists or braids if you will style later.

blocks.text: **Deep conditioning** every two to four weeks gives extra softness. Apply a thick conditioner or hair mask, cover with a plastic cap, and leave for 15 to 30 minutes. Gentle warmth from a warm towel or hooded dryer helps it work, especially on low porosity hair.
LOC and LCO: moisture in, then sealed

Water is the true moisturiser for hair. Oils and butters do not add moisture by themselves; they slow down how fast water leaves the strand. That is why you put water-based products on first and seal afterwards. The two common orders are:

head: Step
LOC method
LCO method
rows: L: Liquid or leave-in (water, leave-in conditioner)
O: Oil (for example jojoba, olive or coconut oil)
C: Cream (a moisturising hair cream or butter blend)
C: Cream to seal and define
O: Oil on top to seal
High porosity or very dry hair
Low porosity hair that feels greasy with oil first

blocks.title: LOC moisture method
items: Damp hair in sections
Liquid or leave-in
Light oil
Cream to seal
Twist or braid
blocks.caption: Each layer has a job: water hydrates, oil and cream slow water loss.

blocks.text: Shea butter, known locally as **ori** in Yoruba and **okwuma** in Igbo, is a popular sealant and is easy to find in Nigerian markets. Use a small amount, warmed between the palms. Too much butter on low porosity hair sits on top and attracts dust.
Relaxed hair needs the same moisture

Relaxed hair is chemically straightened, so it is more porous and weaker at the line where new growth meets relaxed hair. It still needs regular washing, conditioning and moisture. Be extra gentle at that line of demarcation, and avoid heavy heat.
Protecting hair between washes

Moisture escapes most at night, when cotton pillowcases rub the hair and soak up products. Cover the hair with a **satin or silk scarf or bonnet**, or sleep on a satin pillowcase. Between washes, lightly mist the ends with water or a leave-in spray and seal with a little oil every two or three days, or whenever the hair feels dry and stiff. Avoid tight rubber bands with metal joins; use soft scrunchies or fabric ties instead.

blocks.title: Worked example: a simple wash-day budget
blocks.context: For example, Fatima in Kaduna wants a basic home wash-day kit for herself and her two daughters. Prices are approximate and vary by market and brand.
steps: Sulphate-free shampoo, 500 ml: about 4,500 naira (approximate).
Rinse-out conditioner, 500 ml: about 4,000 naira (approximate).
Leave-in conditioner or spray, 250 ml: about 3,500 naira (approximate).
Raw shea butter, 500 g from the market: about 2,500 naira (approximate); spray bottle and wide-tooth comb: about 1,500 naira together (approximate).
Total: about 16,000 naira. If one wash uses about 30 ml shampoo and 50 ml conditioner per head, the bottles last for many washes.
blocks.result: Fatima has a realistic kit that will last the family several weeks, and she knows which item to re-buy first: conditioner, because it is used in the largest amounts.

blocks.title: Read the label, not the advert
blocks.text: Look at the first five ingredients, because they make up most of the product. Water (aqua) first is good for a moisturiser. Check for a NAFDAC registration number on locally sold products, and avoid unlabelled mixtures sold in nylon bags with no name or address.

takeaways: Wash afro-textured hair about every one to two weeks, scalp first
Detangle only with conditioner in, from ends to roots
Water hydrates; oils and butters seal
LOC suits many dry, high porosity heads; LCO often suits low porosity
Check ingredients and NAFDAC numbers on products

activity.title: Do one full wash day
steps: Choose a volunteer (or yourself) and write down the products you will use.
Section, shampoo, condition and detangle following the order in this lesson.
Apply LOC or LCO and finish in six to eight chunky twists or braids.
Note how long each stage took and how the hair felt before and after.
Two days later, ask how soft the hair still feels and write it down.
activity.evidence: Before and after photos (with permission), a list of products used, and your timing notes.

lessons.title: Your tool kit and a hygiene system that prevents infection
objectives: List the essential tools for washing, parting and braiding
Explain the difference between cleaning and disinfecting
Clean, disinfect and store combs and clips correctly
Set up a safe, organised workstation before every client

blocks.text: A client trusts you with her scalp. Combs, clips, towels and hands can carry lice, fungal infections like ringworm, and bacteria from one head to the next. A simple hygiene routine protects your clients, your family and your reputation. It also looks professional, which helps you charge fair prices.
Starter tool kit

head: Tool
What it is for
Approximate cost (naira)
rows: Making clean parts for cornrows and braids
Holding sections out of the way
Trimming ends and extension hair (used only for hair)
Protecting clothes; one clean set per client

blocks.text: All prices above are approximate and vary by city and market. Buy fewer tools of better quality, and keep a set aside so you always have clean ones while another set is soaking.

blocks.name: gloves
blocks.caption: Gloves protect you during chemical work and when cleaning tools with disinfectant.

blocks.text: Cleaning is not the same as disinfecting

items: **Cleaning** removes hair, product and dirt with soap or detergent and water. You must clean first, because disinfectant cannot work through grease and hair.
**Disinfecting** kills most germs on a hard, clean surface using a chemical disinfectant left on for the full contact time stated on the label.
**Sterilising** kills all microbes and needs special equipment such as an autoclave. It is used in clinics, not usually in braiding salons.

blocks.title: Tool hygiene after every client
items: Remove all hair
Wash with soap
Rinse well
Soak for label time
Dry, store covered
blocks.caption: Disinfectant only works on tools that are already clean.

items: Remove hair from combs and brushes straight after the client leaves.
Wash tools in warm water with liquid soap or detergent, scrubbing between the teeth with an old toothbrush.
Rinse and fully immerse them in a salon disinfectant (for example Barbicide) mixed exactly as the label says. Barbicide's label contact time is 10 minutes. For other products, follow their label.
Remove with gloves or tongs, rinse if the label says so, and air dry on a clean towel.
Store in a clean, closed container. Never put used tools back with clean ones.
Change the disinfectant solution as the label instructs, or sooner if it looks cloudy or has hair in it.

blocks.title: Using household bleach
blocks.text: If you use household bleach, dilute it exactly as the bottle instructs for disinfecting, mix a fresh batch each day, wear gloves, and work with a window open. Never mix bleach with ammonia, vinegar or other cleaners, because this releases dangerous gases. Do not soak metal scissors in bleach for long, as it can corrode them.
Your workstation and your hands

Wash your hands with soap and water before and after each client. Use a clean towel and cape for every client, and wash them with detergent before using again. Items that cannot be cleaned, such as cotton wool, used rubber bands and disposable neck strips, are thrown away after one client. Keep food and drinks off the work table, and keep chemicals out of children's reach.

blocks.title: Heat and hot water
blocks.text: Many braiders dip the ends of synthetic braids in hot water to seal them. Pour the water into a stable bowl or mug, never hold the kettle over the client, protect her shoulders and neck with a towel, and keep children well away. If you use a blow dryer, keep it moving, use a medium setting, and keep the cord away from water.

blocks.title: Worked example: setting up a corner salon at home
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi in Enugu wants to start braiding on Saturdays in her parlour. She has 30,000 naira (approximate) to spend on hygiene and tools.
steps: She buys two rat-tail combs, two wide-tooth combs and a pack of clips: about 6,000 naira (approximate).
She buys three capes and six small towels so she can rotate them: about 12,000 naira (approximate).
She buys a lidded plastic container and a bottle of salon disinfectant: about 9,000 naira (approximate).
She keeps 3,000 naira for liquid soap, gloves and a bin with a lid.
She writes a small card on the wall: remove hair, wash, soak for label time, dry, store.
blocks.result: Ngozi spends her 30,000 naira on two sets of tools and enough linen to give every client clean items, which lets her work back-to-back without skipping hygiene.

blocks.title: Lice and fungal infections
blocks.text: If you see live lice or nits, or round scaly patches, stop politely and do not continue the style. Put all tools used into cleaning and disinfection immediately, and wash the cape and towels.

takeaways: Keep two sets of tools so one is always clean
Always clean before you disinfect
Follow the disinfectant label for mixing and contact time
Fresh towel and cape for every client
Stop the service if you see lice or signs of infection

activity.title: Build and test your hygiene station
steps: List the tools you already own and what you still need, with approximate prices from your local market.
Set up a container with disinfectant mixed according to its label.
Clean and disinfect your combs and clips following the six steps in this lesson, timing the soak.
Write the hygiene steps on a card and stick it near your workstation.
activity.evidence: A photo of your organised tool station, your shopping list with prices, and the hygiene card.

quiz.q: A client's 4C hair feels oily at the scalp but very dry at the ends. What is the most likely reason?
options: Sebum cannot travel easily down tightly coiled strands
Her hair is low porosity so it cannot get wet
Shea butter has blocked her follicles
quiz.explain: On coily hair, the natural scalp oil struggles to move past each bend, so the ends stay dry while the scalp is oily.

quiz.q: During detangling, which approach causes the least breakage?
options: Combing dry hair from the roots down
Using fingers then a wide-tooth comb on conditioned hair, from ends to roots
Using a fine-tooth comb on wet hair without product
Brushing hard to remove knots quickly
quiz.explain: Conditioner adds slip, and starting at the ends removes knots without pushing them into a bigger tangle.

quiz.q: Kemi's hair soaks up water fast but feels dry again within hours. She has had relaxers and colour. Which description fits best?
quiz.explain: A raised or damaged cuticle lets water in quickly and out quickly, which is high porosity, common after chemical services.

quiz.q: In the LOC method, what is the job of the oil and cream?
options: They add moisture to the hair
They loosen the curl pattern permanently
They slow down how fast water leaves the strand
quiz.explain: Water is the moisturiser; oil and cream seal it in by slowing water loss.

quiz.q: You have just finished a client. What is the correct first step for her combs?
options: Remove hair, then wash with soap and water
Wipe them with a dry towel and reuse
quiz.explain: Disinfectant cannot work through hair and grease, so tools must be cleaned before they are disinfected.

quiz.q: While parting a child's hair you see round scaly patches with short broken hairs. What should you do?
options: Braid tightly over the patches to hide them
Stop politely, advise a clinic visit, and disinfect all tools used
Cut the hair in that area
quiz.explain: These can be signs of ringworm of the scalp, which spreads through tools and towels. Refer and disinfect.

modules.title: Guided Practice: Consultation, Cornrows, Twists and Braids
modules.overview: Now you put your hands to work. You will learn a repeatable service workflow that starts with a proper consultation, then practise all-back cornrows, two-strand twists and box braids with extensions. Each lesson ends with a practice task and a simple way to collect feedback and improve.

lessons.title: The client service workflow, from consultation to aftercare
objectives: Run a five-minute client consultation and fill a client record card
Check the hair and scalp and decide whether a style is suitable
Follow the same service steps from preparation to finish every time
Give clear aftercare advice and agree a takedown date

blocks.text: Good stylists are not only good with their hands. They ask the right questions before they start, so there are no surprises about the style, the time, the price or the client's comfort. A clear workflow also helps you work faster, because you are not stopping to decide what to do next.

blocks.name: conversation
blocks.alt: Two people talking face to face
blocks.caption: A short, honest consultation prevents most complaints before the first part is made.

blocks.text: The consultation questions

items: **What style, size and length do you want?** Ask for a photo, and agree what is realistic for her hair length and density.
**When was your last chemical service?** Relaxer, texturiser, colour or keratin treatment in the last two weeks changes what is safe.
**Any allergies, scalp conditions or sensitive areas?** Ask about itching, tenderness, past reactions to extension hair or products.
**How long do you plan to keep it?** This helps you advise on braid size and aftercare.
**Budget and time**: tell her the price, whether it includes extension hair, and roughly how many hours it will take.

head: Client card field
Example entry
rows: 4B/4C, medium density, dry ends, thin at temples
Relaxed 9 months ago, now mostly natural
Itchy with some synthetic hair; mild dandruff
Medium knotless braids, waist length, client brings 4 packs

blocks.text: Keep cards in a notebook or a simple phone note. Treat this information as private: under the **Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023**, personal information should be collected for a clear purpose and protected. Do not share a client's photos or details in WhatsApp status without her permission.
Check before you agree

Look at the hairline, crown and nape with good light. If the edges are thin, choose bigger braids at the front, leave out the edges, or suggest a style with less weight. If the hair is very short, explain that some styles will not hold yet. If the scalp shows signs of infection, open sores or a recent chemical burn, do not continue; suggest a clinic.

blocks.title: The service workflow
items: Consult and record
Check hair and scalp
Wash and stretch
Part and style
Finish and aftercare
blocks.caption: Following the same five stages every time makes your work consistent and your timing predictable.

blocks.text: The service steps

items: Wash your hands, set out clean tools, cape and towel.
Wash, condition and detangle the hair (or confirm the client arrived with clean, detangled hair).
Moisturise and **stretch** the hair. Coily hair shrinks a lot; stretching with large twists, braids or a blow dryer on medium heat makes parting easier.
Map the style: decide the direction and number of rows or braids before making the first part.
Style in sections, keeping the rest of the hair clipped away and lightly damp.
Check the finish: parts, size, ends, edges. Show the client the back with a hand mirror.
Give aftercare advice and book or suggest the takedown date.

blocks.text: Working on children's hair

When the client is a child, the consultation is with the parent or guardian, and the child's comfort comes first. Children's scalps are tender, and their edges are easily damaged. Choose bigger, lighter styles, use little or no extension hair, and allow short breaks. If a child cries from pain, the braid is too tight, so loosen it. Do not apply relaxers or other chemical straighteners to a child's hair as part of a basic service.

blocks.title: Worked example: timing a Saturday booking
blocks.context: For example, Halima in Kano has a client booked at 10 a.m. for medium knotless braids to mid-back. She wants to know when she can take the next client.
steps: Consultation and scalp check: 10 minutes.
Client arrived with washed hair, so Halima applies leave-in and blow dries on medium to stretch: 40 minutes.
Parting and braiding about 120 braids at roughly 2 minutes each: 240 minutes, or 4 hours.
Sealing ends, final check and aftercare talk: 20 minutes.
Total: 10 + 40 + 240 + 20 = 310 minutes, about 5 hours 10 minutes.
blocks.result: The client should finish around 3:10 p.m. Halima books the next client for 4 p.m., giving time to clean tools, eat and rest her hands.

blocks.text: Aftercare advice to give every client

items: Sleep with a satin scarf or bonnet.
Moisturise the scalp and braids lightly every few days; do not pile heavy grease on the scalp.
If braids feel painful, cause bumps or pull the edges after the first day, come back to loosen them.
Take the style down within the advised time, usually between four and eight weeks, so new growth does not tangle and matt.

blocks.title: Agree the price before you start
blocks.text: Say the price clearly, say whether extension hair is included, and agree payment method (cash or transfer to your Moniepoint, Opay or bank account). Confirm the transfer has arrived in your own banking app, not from a screenshot the client shows you.

takeaways: Every service starts with a consultation and a client card
Never continue over infection, open sores or a fresh chemical burn
Stretch coily hair before parting for cleaner results
Time each stage so you can book clients realistically
Protect client privacy and get permission before posting photos

activity.title: Run a real consultation
steps: Make a client card template in your notebook or phone with the seven fields in this lesson.
Consult one volunteer using the five questions, and fill in the card.
Check her hairline, crown and nape and write what style size you would advise and why.
Estimate the time for her chosen style stage by stage.
activity.evidence: A completed client card (with the volunteer's permission) and your written time estimate.

lessons.title: All-back cornrows, step by step
objectives: Part straight, even rows using a rat-tail comb
Braid an underhand cornrow while picking up hair along the row
Keep tension firm but comfortable, especially at the hairline
Finish and check a full head of all-back cornrows

blocks.text: Cornrows are braids made flat against the scalp. In Nigeria they are often called **shuku** when they gather at the top, or all-back when they run from the front to the nape. They are the base skill for many other styles, including sew-in weaves and some wigs, so getting them neat and comfortable is worth practising until it feels natural.

blocks.name: haircut-female-sign
blocks.alt: A woman having her hair styled
blocks.caption: Cornrows are a core skill: neat parts and steady hands matter more than speed at first.

blocks.text: Underhand versus overhand

A cornrow is a three-strand braid. In the **underhand** method, you cross the outer strands under the middle strand each time. This makes the braid stand up on top of the scalp, which is the classic cornrow look. In the **overhand** method, you cross over the middle, and the braid lies flatter and looks like a French braid. Most cornrows are done underhand.

blocks.title: Underhand vs overhand braiding
items: Underhand (cornrow)
Overhand (French style)
blocks.caption: The direction you cross the strands changes how the braid sits on the scalp.

blocks.text: Before you start

items: Hair should be clean, detangled, moisturised and stretched.
Have a rat-tail comb, clips, spray bottle and a light gel or braiding cream for grip.
Seat the client so her head is at your chest height. Bending for hours hurts your back and makes your rows uneven.
Decide the number of rows. For a beginner all-back style, 8 to 12 rows is manageable.

blocks.text: Braiding one row

items: With the tail of the comb, part a straight line from the front hairline to the nape. Part a second line parallel to it, the width you want the row. Clip the rest of the hair away.
Apply a little gel or cream along the row to control frizz and give grip.
At the hairline, take a small piece of hair and divide it into three equal strands: left, middle and right.
Cross the left strand under the middle. Now cross the right strand under the new middle. This is your first stitch.
Before each next cross, use your index finger to pick up a small amount of loose hair from the row just next to the strand, and add it to that outer strand. Then cross it under the middle.
Keep your hands close to the scalp and move along the row, adding hair each time, until you reach the nape.
When there is no more loose hair to pick up, continue a normal three-strand braid to the ends and secure with a small band or by twisting the ends.

blocks.text: Tension: firm, never painful

A cornrow should feel snug, not painful. If the client winces, if you see small white bumps, or if the scalp lifts like a tent around the base of the braid, the tension is too high. Pull hardest in the middle of the head and gentlest at the hairline and temples, where hair is finest. Dermatologists warn that repeated tight styling can lead to **traction alopecia**, hair loss from constant pulling, which can become permanent if it continues for years.

blocks.title: Worked example: planning a ten-row all-back
blocks.context: For example, Esther in Ibadan is practising on her younger sister, whose hairline measures about 25 cm from ear to ear across the front.
steps: She wants 10 rows, so she divides 25 cm by 10: each row starts about 2.5 cm wide at the hairline.
She marks the centre part first, then works out to each side, so the rows on the left and right match.
Her first rows take about 12 minutes each. By row 6 she is down to about 8 minutes.
Total time: about 10 rows x 10 minutes average = 100 minutes, plus 20 minutes preparation.
blocks.result: Esther finishes in about 2 hours, with rows matched on both sides because she started from the centre and measured.

blocks.text: Common beginner problems and fixes

head: Problem
Likely cause
Fix
rows: Row gets wider towards the nape
Picking up too much hair on each cross
Pick up smaller, equal amounts; check the part lines first
Gaps or loops under the braid
Hands moving away from the scalp
Keep your knuckles close to the scalp and pull each strand down along the row
Hair too dry or not stretched
Mist lightly, use a little gel or cream, stretch before parting
Stretch, comb flat and part with the comb tail in one smooth line

blocks.title: Practise on a mannequin head first
blocks.text: A training mannequin head with afro-textured hair lets you practise parting and tension without tiring a real person. Clamp it to a table at chest height and practise for 30 minutes a day.

When the full style is done, check that parts are straight, rows are the same width on both sides, the edges are not pulled, and the ends are secure. Hold a hand mirror so the client can see the back, and ask if any row feels tight.

takeaways: Most cornrows are underhand: outer strands cross under the middle
Add a small, equal amount of hair on every cross for an even row
Measure and start from the centre so both sides match
Firm but not painful; be gentlest at the edges
Pain, bumps or tenting mean the braid is too tight

activity.title: Braid a full all-back
steps: Prepare a mannequin head or a willing volunteer with clean, stretched hair.
Measure the hairline and plan 8 to 12 rows.
Braid all rows underhand, timing each row.
Ask the volunteer to rate comfort from 1 to 5 and check for tight spots.
Photograph the front, both sides and the back.
activity.evidence: Four photos of the finished style, your row-by-row times, and the comfort rating.

lessons.title: Two-strand twists, box braids and your practice feedback loop
objectives: Make two-strand twists on natural hair
Install box braids with extension hair using even square parts
Seal synthetic ends safely
Collect specific feedback and improve one weak point at a time

blocks.text: Twists and box braids are among the most requested protective styles. **Protective styles** keep the ends of the hair tucked away and reduce daily combing, which can help retain length. They only protect the hair if they are not too tight, not too heavy and not left in too long.

blocks.name: black-scissors
blocks.caption: Sharp scissors kept only for hair give clean, even ends on twists and braids.

blocks.text: Two-strand twists (natural hair, no extensions)

items: Start with clean, detangled, moisturised hair. Twists hold best on slightly damp hair with a twisting cream.
Part a small square section and comb it smooth.
Divide it into two equal strands.
Wrap one strand over the other, twisting each strand slightly in the same direction as you go, down to the ends.
Coil the ends around your finger to help them hold. Repeat across the head, working back to front or front to back in neat rows.

blocks.text: Box braids with extension hair

Box braids are three-strand braids that hang freely, with square or rectangular parts. Extension hair, usually a synthetic fibre such as pre-stretched braid hair, adds length and thickness. Knotless braids start with the client's own hair and add extension gradually with small feed-ins, so there is less weight on the root at the start.

items: Part the hair into rows, then part each row into squares of equal size. Use a ruler or your fingertip as a guide.
Take a piece of extension hair in proportion to the section. Too much extension on a small section pulls and can damage the root.

For a classic box braid, fold the extension around the base of the client's hair and braid three strands, keeping her hair mixed into two of them. For knotless, start braiding her own hair for two or three stitches, then feed in small pieces of extension.
Braid down to the length wanted with even tension.
Seal the ends: carefully dip synthetic ends in hot water from a stable bowl, then blot with a towel. Some fibres need a band or a twist instead.

blocks.title: Practice feedback loop
items: Do one practice style
Photograph and time it
Ask for specific feedback
Fix one weak point
Practise again
blocks.caption: Improving one thing at a time is faster than trying to fix everything at once.

blocks.text: Getting feedback that helps
"It's fine" teaches you nothing. Ask specific questions and score yourself the same way every time, so you can see progress across practice sessions.

head: Check
Score 1 to 5
What a 5 looks like
rows: Straight, even squares or rows, no zig-zags
All braids the same thickness from front to back
No pain, no bumps, edges not pulled

blocks.title: Worked example: improving parts over three sessions
blocks.context: For example, Rukayat in Abeokuta practises medium box braids on her cousin every Sunday and scores each session with the table above.
steps: Session 1: parts score 2, size 3, comfort 4, ends 3, time 6 hours. She chooses parts as her one weak point.
Before session 2 she practises parting only on a mannequin for 20 minutes a day and uses a ruler for the first row.
Session 2: parts score 4, size 3, comfort 4, ends 3, time 5 hours 30 minutes. Her next focus is braid size.
She cuts and weighs extension pieces before starting so each braid gets the same amount.
Session 3: parts 4, size 4, comfort 5, ends 4, time 5 hours.
blocks.result: Her total score rose from 12 to 17 out of 20 (excluding time) and she saved an hour, by fixing one weak point per session.

blocks.text: Taking braids down safely

items: Cut the extension hair just below where the client's own hair ends. Feel for her ends before cutting.
Unbraid each braid gently from the bottom up, using the tail of a comb to separate strands.
At the root, there will be shed hair and product build-up. Do not rip it out: apply a little oil or conditioner and loosen it with your fingers.
Detangle each section with fingers and a wide-tooth comb before washing, so shed hair does not matt during the wash.
Wash, deep condition and let the hair and scalp rest for a few days, or at least moisturise well, before the next protective style.

blocks.title: Weight and length
blocks.text: Very long or very thick braids are heavy and pull on the roots for weeks. On fine hair or thin edges, suggest shorter length, slightly bigger parts, or knotless braids, and leave the finest edge hairs out.

Some clients react to synthetic extension hair with an itchy, red scalp. Ask about past reactions in the consultation. Some braiders rinse synthetic hair in a mild vinegar and water solution and let it dry fully before installing; if a client has a strong reaction, advise her to take the braids out and see a doctor.

takeaways: Protective styles help only when they are light, comfortable and taken down on time
Equal square parts and equal extension amounts give even braids
Seal synthetic ends with hot water carefully, away from the skin
Score each practice style the same way and fix one weak point at a time

activity.title: Practise and score
steps: Do a section of at least 20 two-strand twists or 20 box braids on a volunteer or mannequin.
Time yourself and take photos.
Score yourself using the five-row table, then ask the volunteer to score comfort.
Choose one weak point, practise it for a week, and repeat the section.
activity.evidence: Photos and scores from two practice sessions, with a one-paragraph note on what improved.

quiz.q: A client wants braids today but tells you she relaxed her hair four days ago and her scalp still stings in one area. What should you do?
options: Braid tightly so the style lasts
Postpone, avoid the sore area, and suggest she sees a doctor if it does not settle
Apply gel to the sore area and continue
Do the style but charge more
quiz.explain: A stinging scalp after a recent chemical service may be a chemical burn. Braiding over it adds tension and risk.

quiz.q: Why should you stretch coily hair before parting cornrows?
options: It changes the curl pattern permanently
It reduces shrinkage so parts are cleaner and braiding is easier
It makes the hair grow faster
quiz.explain: Coily hair shrinks a lot. Stretching makes it easier to part and braid neatly.

quiz.q: In an underhand cornrow, what do you do with the outer strands?
options: Cross them under the middle, adding hair each time
quiz.explain: Underhand means outer strands go under the middle strand, which makes the braid sit raised on the scalp.

quiz.q: A client says her new cornrows hurt and you see small white bumps along the hairline. What is the best response?
options: Loosen or redo the tight rows at the hairline
Tell her it will loosen in a week
quiz.explain: Pain and bumps are signs of too much tension, which can lead to traction alopecia. Loosen the affected rows.

quiz.q: Halima plans 100 braids at about 3 minutes each, plus 30 minutes preparation and 15 minutes finishing. About how long is the service?
quiz.explain: 100 x 3 = 300 minutes, plus 30 and 15 = 345 minutes, which is 5 hours 45 minutes.

quiz.q: Rukayat's practice scores are: parts 2, size 3, comfort 4, ends 3. What should she focus on next?
quiz.explain: The feedback loop works best by fixing the weakest point first, then moving to the next.

modules.title: Quality, Chemical Safety and Keeping Good Records
modules.overview: A style that looks good on day one but breaks hair by week six is not good work. This module sets a clear quality standard, teaches the safety rules for chemical relaxers and how to handle clients fairly, and shows you how to track your time, money and repeat clients in a simple record.

lessons.title: Quality standards and the mistakes that damage hair
objectives: Use a six-point quality checklist on every finished style
Spot the early signs of traction alopecia
Correct the most common styling mistakes before the client leaves
Explain to clients why some popular habits cause breakage

blocks.text: Clients judge your work in two moments: when they look in the mirror on the day, and when they take the style down weeks later. Neat parts win the first moment. Healthy edges and a comfortable scalp win the second, and that is what brings them back and makes them recommend you.

blocks.name: mirror
blocks.caption: Always show the client the back and sides with a mirror, and fix what you both see before she leaves.

blocks.text: The six-point finish check

blocks.title: Finish check before the client leaves
items: Parts straight and even
Braids same size
Comfortable, no pain
Edges not pulled
Ends neat and sealed
Scalp clean, no residue
blocks.caption: Run this check every time, even when you are tired or the client is in a hurry.

blocks.text: Do the check standing back first, about an arm's length away, to see the overall shape. Then look closely at the hairline, the nape and behind the ears, the areas beginners rush. Ask the client to move her head side to side and look up and down, because tight braids often only hurt when she moves.
Traction alopecia: the damage to prevent

Traction alopecia is hair loss caused by repeated pulling on the hair roots. It usually shows first at the temples, the front hairline and around the ears. Early on it can recover if the pulling stops. If tight styles continue for a long time, the follicles can scar and the hair may not grow back. It is one of the most common causes of thin edges seen by dermatologists in women of African descent.

items: **Warning signs during or after styling**: pain, a stinging or burning feeling, headaches, small bumps or pimples at the base of braids, scalp lifting like a tent around the braid, and redness.
**Longer-term signs**: thinning or receding edges, short broken hairs along the hairline, and shiny patches where hair no longer grows.
**Higher-risk combinations**: tight braids on relaxed hair, heavy extensions on small sections, the same tight ponytail or bun every day, and glue-on hair applied to the hairline.

blocks.title: "It will loosen" is not an answer
blocks.text: Never send a client home with braids that hurt and tell her the pain will pass. If a braid hurts, loosen or redo it. Pain is the hair root being pulled, and the damage builds every day the style stays in.
Common mistakes and how to correct them

head: Mistake
Why it is a problem
What to do instead
rows: Braiding the edges very tight for a sleek look
The finest hairs carry the most stress
Use lighter tension at the front, leave baby hairs out, or start braids slightly back
Too much extension hair on a small section
Weight pulls the root for weeks
Match extension amount to section size; make bigger parts for long styles
Leaving styles in for three months or more
New growth tangles, matts and breaks at takedown
Advise takedown within about four to eight weeks
Build-up, itching and blocked hair under braids
Light oil or a scalp spray, used sparingly
Detangle with conditioner or leave-in, ends to roots
High heat to straighten before braiding
Can burn the cuticle and cause permanent heat damage
Use stretching methods or a blow dryer on medium heat, with a heat protectant

blocks.text: Habits to explain to clients
Much damage happens at home between appointments. Give clients short, clear advice when they ask how to keep their hair healthy:

items: Do not wear the same tight ponytail, bun or wig grip every day; change the pulling point.
Avoid sleeping in rollers or tight bands; use a satin scarf instead.
Limit flat irons and hot combs, and never use them on wet hair.
Do not scratch the scalp with nails or combs under braids; pat or use a light scalp spray instead.
Take styles down on time, and rest the hair for a few days between long protective styles.

blocks.title: Worked example: fixing a style before the client leaves
blocks.context: For example, Grace in Port Harcourt has just finished feed-in cornrows for her client Ifeoma. During the finish check, Ifeoma says the two front rows by her temples feel very tight.
steps: Grace looks closely and sees slight tenting at the base of both front rows.
She undoes the first 5 cm of each row, mists the hair and re-braids with lighter tension, starting about half a centimetre behind the finest edge hairs.
The fix takes 15 minutes. Ifeoma moves her head in all directions and says it now feels comfortable.
Grace notes on Ifeoma's client card: temples sensitive, lighter tension at front.
blocks.result: Ifeoma leaves comfortable, Grace protects her edges, and the note means the next appointment starts right.

blocks.text: Quality also includes timing and honesty. If a style will take longer than you said, tell the client early. If her hair is too short or fragile for the look she wants, say so kindly and suggest an alternative. A small loss of income today is better than a client with damaged edges telling her friends where she got her braids.

takeaways: Check parts, size, comfort, edges, ends and scalp before she leaves
Pain, bumps and tenting are warning signs, not normal
Traction alopecia can become permanent if pulling continues
Lighter tension at the hairline; extension weight matched to section size
Record sensitive areas on the client card

activity.title: Audit your own work
steps: Take your photos from the Module 2 practice styles.
Score each one using the six-point finish check (1 to 5 for each point).
Identify the lowest-scoring point and write what caused it.
Write one change you will make next time, and a sentence you will use to explain to clients why you will not braid the edges tight.
activity.evidence: Your completed six-point scores for two styles and the written improvement plan.

lessons.title: Chemical relaxer safety, consent and fair treatment
objectives: Explain how lye and no-lye relaxers work and their main risks
Follow the key safety steps for a relaxer retouch
Get informed consent and know when to refuse a chemical service
Handle complaints, children and privacy fairly

blocks.text: Relaxers are still common in Nigerian salons. They permanently straighten afro-textured hair by breaking bonds inside the cortex. Because they are strong alkaline chemicals, they can cause scalp burns, eye injuries and severe breakage when used wrongly. This lesson gives you the core safety rules. Before you offer relaxers as a paid service, train with an experienced stylist and always follow the manufacturer's instructions for the exact product you use.

blocks.name: warning-sign
blocks.caption: Relaxers are strong alkaline chemicals: treat every application as a safety procedure.

blocks.text: Lye and no-lye relaxers

blocks.title: Lye vs no-lye relaxers
items: Lye relaxer
No-lye relaxer
blocks.caption: No-lye does not mean no chemical: both are strong alkalis that need the same care.

blocks.text: **Lye relaxers** use sodium hydroxide, the same caustic soda used in soap making. **No-lye relaxers** usually use guanidine hydroxide (made by mixing calcium hydroxide cream with a guanidine carbonate activator) or another hydroxide. No-lye products are often marketed as milder for the scalp, but they can leave mineral deposits that make hair dry and dull unless washed out with a chelating shampoo. Both can burn and both can break hair.
Safety steps for a relaxer retouch

items: **Consult and check the scalp.** Do not relax if there are cuts, sores, scratches, irritation or a recent hair loss problem. Ask the client not to scratch, brush hard or wash her scalp for a day or two before the appointment.
**Strand test.** Follow the product's instructions to test a small hidden section, to see how the hair responds and how long it needs.
**Protect yourself and the client.** Wear gloves, put a cape and towel on the client, and protect her hairline, ears and scalp with a petroleum base cream.
**Apply only to new growth.** Relax only the untreated new growth, not the hair that was relaxed before. Overlapping onto old relaxed hair causes breakage.
**Time it exactly.** Use a timer and never exceed the time on the label. If the client says it burns, rinse immediately, do not wait.
**Rinse thoroughly and neutralise.** Rinse with plenty of lukewarm water, then use the neutralising shampoo that comes with the kit, repeating as the instructions say, until all relaxer is gone.
**Condition and record.** Apply conditioner, then record the product, timing and any reactions on the client card.

blocks.title: Eyes and burns
blocks.text: If relaxer gets into the eyes, rinse immediately with plenty of clean running water for at least 15 minutes and get medical help. If the scalp burns or blisters, rinse at once with lots of water and advise a clinic visit. Keep relaxers locked away from children.

Most stylists space relaxer retouches about 8 to 10 weeks apart or longer, and avoid colouring and relaxing on the same day. Many advise waiting about two weeks between a relaxer and colour, and between a relaxer and tight braids, so the scalp and hair can recover.

blocks.title: Health questions from clients
blocks.text: In 2022, the US National Institutes of Health reported a study that linked frequent use of chemical hair straighteners with a higher risk of uterine cancer. Studies like this show an association, not proof that relaxers cause cancer. If a client asks, share that research exists, do not make medical claims, and respect her choice to go natural or keep relaxing.
Consent, fairness and privacy

items: **Informed consent**: before a chemical service, explain the risks in plain words and let her decide. Write "risks explained, client agreed" on the card with the date.
**Children**: do not apply relaxers or chemical straighteners to children as part of this basic course's services.
**Fair treatment**: give every client the same quality and honesty, whatever her age, size, hair texture or ability to pay.
**Privacy**: keep client cards safe, and only post photos she has agreed to, with her face hidden if she prefers.

blocks.text: Handling a complaint

items: Listen fully without interrupting, and look at the problem together in good light.
If it is a safety issue (pain, burning, bumps, blisters), fix it or refer to a clinic first, before discussing money.
If the style has a fault you caused, such as uneven braids or a loose row, offer to redo that part free.
Record the complaint and what you did on the client card, so you learn from it.

blocks.title: Worked example: deciding to postpone
blocks.context: For example, Adaeze in Owerri has a regular client, Nkem, booked for a relaxer retouch. During the consultation, Nkem mentions she scratched her scalp a lot last night because of dandruff.
steps: Adaeze parts the hair and sees small scratch marks and redness near the crown.
She explains that relaxer on scratched skin can cause a painful burn.
She offers a gentle wash, conditioning treatment and a simple twist-out today instead, for her normal wash price.
She rebooks the relaxer for one week later and advises Nkem not to scratch, and to see a pharmacist or doctor about the dandruff if it continues.
blocks.result: Nkem leaves with clean, styled hair and no burn. She trusts Adaeze more because she put her safety ahead of the bigger sale.

takeaways: Lye and no-lye relaxers are both strong alkalis that can burn
Never relax over cuts, scratches or irritation
Apply only to new growth, time exactly, rinse and neutralise fully
Explain risks and record consent before chemical services
No relaxers on children in this basic service

activity.title: Write your chemical safety card
steps: Choose one relaxer product sold in your local market and read its full instructions.
Write the product's strand test, timing and neutralising steps in your own words.
Add the seven safety steps from this lesson and the eye and burn first aid.
Write a short consent sentence you will read to clients before any chemical service.
activity.evidence: A photo of your handwritten or typed safety and consent card, with the product name and its timing.

lessons.title: Tracking time, money and repeat clients
objectives: Keep a simple service log for every client
Calculate your cost, profit and earnings per hour for a style
Track repeat clients and the source of new clients
Write a short monthly report that another person can understand

blocks.text: Many talented braiders are always busy but never seem to have money. Usually the reason is simple: they do not know how long each style really takes, what it costs them, or which styles actually pay. A few numbers, written down after every client, change that.

blocks.name: data-reports
blocks.alt: A person reviewing charts and reports
blocks.caption: A simple log turns busy days into clear numbers you can act on.

blocks.text: The service log
Use a notebook, a free spreadsheet app such as Google Sheets, or a notes app. Fill one line per client, straight after she leaves.
These example figures are approximate and only for practice. Your prices will depend on your area, your skill and your client base.
Four numbers to watch

items: **Profit per service** = price minus materials (gel, cream, bands, extension hair if you supply it, disinfectant share).
**Earnings per hour** = profit divided by hours. This shows which styles truly pay.
**Repeat rate** = repeat clients divided by total clients in the month. A rising repeat rate means clients trust your work.
**Client sources**: count how new clients found you, so you put your effort where it works.

blocks.text: Costs beginners forget

items: Disinfectant, gloves and liquid soap used across many clients: divide the monthly spend by the number of clients.
Washing capes and towels: detergent and water.
Transport, if you do home service: add it to the price for that client.
Data for WhatsApp and photos, and electricity or fuel for a blow dryer.
Replacing combs, clips and scissors every few months.

blocks.text: A simple way to include these is to add up all such costs for one month and divide by the number of clients. For example, if these costs come to about 11,000 naira (approximate) in a month with 22 clients, add about 500 naira to the materials figure for each client.

blocks.title: From log to decision
items: Log every client
Total each month
Work out four numbers
Spot what pays
Adjust prices or focus
blocks.caption: Numbers are only useful when they lead to a decision.

blocks.title: Worked example: which style pays best?
blocks.context: For example, Bisi in Lagos looks at her log for September. Figures are approximate.
steps: All-back cornrows: 12 clients at 5,000 naira, about 300 naira materials each, 1.5 hours each. Profit per client = 4,700. Per hour = 4,700 / 1.5 = about 3,130 naira.
Medium knotless (client brings hair): 4 clients at 20,000 naira, 800 materials, 5 hours. Profit = 19,200. Per hour = 19,200 / 5 = 3,840 naira.
Wash and twists: 6 clients at 7,000 naira, 900 materials, 2.5 hours. Profit = 6,100. Per hour = 6,100 / 2.5 = 2,440 naira.
Total clients: 22. Repeat clients: 9. Repeat rate = 9 / 22 = about 41 percent.
Most new clients came from WhatsApp status (8) and friends (4).
blocks.result: Knotless braids pay best per hour, and wash and twists pay least. Bisi decides to raise her wash-and-twist price a little, promote knotless braids on WhatsApp, and keep cornrows as a quick service that brings repeat clients.

blocks.text: Writing a one-page monthly report
If you work with a partner, a cooperative, a WODDI mentor, or you want a loan, a short report shows that you run a real business. Keep it to five parts, in plain sentences:

items: **Activity**: number of clients and services done this month.
**Money**: total income, total materials and other costs, and profit.
**Quality**: any complaints, redos or safety issues, and what you changed.
**Clients**: repeat rate and the top two client sources.
**Next month**: one or two clear targets, such as "25 clients" or "post three portfolio photos a week".

blocks.text: Read your report once a month and ask three questions. Which style earns the most per hour? Where do my new clients come from? What one problem showed up more than once? Then choose one change only, such as a price adjustment, more photos of your best-paying style, or a slower, gentler hairline technique, and check next month whether it worked.

blocks.title: Separate your money
blocks.text: Use a separate account or wallet for salon income, for example on Moniepoint, Opay or your bank app. Pay yourself a fixed amount weekly. Mixing salon money with house money makes it impossible to see if the business is growing.

blocks.title: Payment scams
blocks.text: Fake transfer alerts and edited screenshots are common. Before a client leaves, confirm the money in your own banking app. Never share your PIN, OTP or card details with anyone who calls claiming to be your bank.

takeaways: Log every client: style, hours, price, materials, payment, source
Earnings per hour shows which styles truly pay
Repeat rate is a simple measure of client trust
A one-page report has activity, money, quality, clients and next targets
Keep salon money separate and confirm transfers in your own app

activity.title: Start your service log
steps: Set up the nine-column log in a notebook or Google Sheets.
Record every practice or paid client for the next two weeks, including volunteers (price zero).
Calculate profit per service and earnings per hour for each style.
Write a short report using the five parts in this lesson.
activity.evidence: A photo or screenshot of your log with at least five entries, and your short report.

quiz.q: During the finish check, a client says her braids only hurt when she looks down. What should you do?
options: Ignore it, since it only hurts sometimes
Find and loosen the braids pulling at the nape or crown
quiz.explain: Pain on movement means some braids are too tight. Loosen them before she leaves to prevent traction damage.

quiz.q: Which situation carries the highest risk of traction alopecia?
options: Loose twists on natural hair for four weeks
Tight, heavy braids on small sections of relaxed hair at the hairline
quiz.explain: Tight tension, heavy weight, small sections, relaxed hair and the fragile hairline all add up to high risk.

quiz.q: During a relaxer retouch, the client says the relaxer is burning. What should you do?
options: Rinse immediately with plenty of water
Add more base cream on top
quiz.explain: Burning means the chemical is injuring the scalp. Rinse at once; do not wait for the timer.

quiz.q: Why should relaxer be applied only to new growth during a retouch?
options: Overlapping onto previously relaxed hair causes over-processing and breakage
New growth is easier to see
quiz.explain: Previously relaxed hair is already weakened; relaxing it again causes over-processing and breakage.

quiz.q: A style costs 600 naira in materials, sells for 12,000 naira and takes 4 hours. What are the earnings per hour?
quiz.explain: Profit = 12,000 minus 600 = 11,400. Divided by 4 hours = 2,850 naira per hour.

quiz.q: Out of 30 clients this month, 12 were repeat clients. What is the repeat rate?
quiz.explain: 12 divided by 30 is 0.4, which is 40 percent.

modules.title: Portfolio, Pricing and Your First 90 Days in Business
modules.overview: In this final module you turn practice into proof and proof into paying clients. You will build a photo portfolio with client consent, set prices that cover your costs and your time, present your services clearly on WhatsApp, and finish with a certification checklist and a realistic 90-day plan.

lessons.title: Building your portfolio project
objectives: Plan a portfolio of at least five finished styles on real heads
Take clear before, during and after photos with a phone
Get and record client consent for every photo used
Present each style with a short, honest description

blocks.text: A portfolio is your proof. New clients cannot feel how gentle your hands are or check your hygiene before they book, but they can see clean parts, healthy edges and neat ends in good photos. Your capstone project for this course is a portfolio of real work, with the records behind it.

blocks.name: mobile-photos
blocks.alt: A woman taking photos with a phone
blocks.caption: A phone camera, good daylight and a plain background are enough for strong portfolio photos.

blocks.text: What goes in the portfolio

items: **At least five finished styles** on at least three different people, covering what you will sell: for example all-back cornrows, two-strand twists and box or knotless braids.
**One full wash-day service** with before and after photos.
**For each style**: a client card (with permission), the time taken, the six-point finish check score, and the client's comfort rating.
**Your hygiene station photo** and your chemical safety card from Module 3.
**A short reflection** on feedback you received and what you changed.

blocks.text: Taking good photos with a phone

items: Use daylight from a window or outdoors in the shade. Avoid direct midday sun, which creates harsh shadows, and avoid yellow bulbs at night.
Use a plain background: a clean wall or a sheet of plain fabric.
Clean the camera lens with a soft cloth before every session.
Take the same angles every time: front, left side, right side, back, and a close-up of the parts and hairline.
Hold the phone at the height of the hair, not from above, and tap the screen on the hair to focus.
Take a 'before' set too, from the same angles, so the change is clear.

blocks.title: Portfolio photo set for one client
items: Before: four angles
During: parting close-up
After: four angles
Hairline close-up
Day 7 check photo
blocks.caption: The same sequence for every client makes your portfolio look consistent and professional.

blocks.text: A photo taken a week later is powerful. It shows that your styles stay neat and that the hairline is calm, with no bumps or redness. Ask clients to send one by WhatsApp in exchange for a small discount on their next visit.
Consent and privacy

Ask permission before you take any photo, and again before you post it. Some clients are happy to show their face; others prefer the back of the head only. Write the answer on the client card, for example: "Photos OK for portfolio and WhatsApp status, no face." For children, ask the parent, and do not show the child's face publicly. Delete photos if a client changes her mind.
Common portfolio mistakes

items: Messy backgrounds such as unmade beds, kitchen pots or other people in the frame.
Photos taken only from the front, which hide the back where most uneven parts show.
Blurry close-ups because the lens was dirty or the phone moved.
Photos of styles you did not do, or styles copied from the internet. This is dishonest and clients will notice when your work looks different.
No record behind the photo: without the client card, time and finish check, a photo alone does not prove safe, repeatable work.

blocks.title: Worked example: a two-week portfolio plan
blocks.context: For example, Joy in Jos needs five portfolio styles in two weeks while still working her weekday job.
steps: She offers three friends and two church members a free or reduced-price style in exchange for photos and honest feedback.
Weekend 1: Saturday, all-back cornrows (2 hours) and wash and twists (2.5 hours). Sunday afternoon, medium box braids (5 hours).
Weekend 2: Saturday, knotless braids on client's own hair (5 hours). Sunday, feed-in cornrows (2.5 hours).
She spends about 3,000 naira (approximate) on gel, bands and a plain backdrop cloth, and takes the same photo set each time.
She collects day-7 photos by WhatsApp and fills a client card and finish-check score for every style.
blocks.result: In two weekends Joy has five documented styles, about 17 hours of practice, and five people who have seen her work and can recommend her.

blocks.title: Be honest in your descriptions
blocks.text: Write simple captions such as "Medium knotless braids, waist length, 5 hours, client's own extension hair." Do not use edited photos that change the hair, and do not claim products or styles make hair grow. Honest captions build trust and reduce disappointed clients.

Your portfolio will keep growing after the course. Every month, replace weaker photos with better ones, and keep at least one example of each service on your price list. If you add a new style, practise it on volunteers first and add it to the portfolio only when it scores well on your finish check.

Store your portfolio in a dedicated phone album and back it up to Google Photos or Google Drive, so you do not lose it if your phone is damaged or stolen. Choose your best eight to ten photos for a WhatsApp Business catalogue, and keep the full records for your certificate submission.

takeaways: Five or more documented styles on at least three people
Same photo angles, daylight and plain background every time
A day-7 photo proves your styles last and edges stay healthy
Record consent; hide faces when asked; protect children's privacy
Back up your portfolio and write honest captions

activity.title: Plan and start your portfolio
steps: List the five styles you will include and the people you will ask.
Book dates and times for each style over the next two to three weeks.
Prepare a plain backdrop and practise the photo angles on one finished style.
Create a phone album named for your portfolio and back it up.
activity.evidence: Your written portfolio plan with names (first names only), dates and styles, plus one complete photo set.

lessons.title: Pricing your services and presenting them to clients
objectives: Calculate a price that covers materials, overheads and your time
Compare your prices with local market rates
Present a clear price list on WhatsApp Business
Explain the value of your service in a short, honest message

blocks.text: Pricing too low is one of the most common reasons small salons struggle. A low price fills your diary but leaves you tired and broke, and it can make clients doubt your quality. A good price covers your materials, your share of costs, and a fair pay for your hours, and still makes sense in your local market.

blocks.name: money-bag
blocks.caption: Your price must pay for materials, costs and your time, not just the products.

blocks.text: A simple pricing formula

items: **Materials**: everything used on that client (gel, cream, bands, extension hair if you supply it).
**Overhead share**: your monthly costs (disinfectant, linen washing, data, transport, tool replacement, rent if any) divided by the number of clients you expect.
**Your time**: hours the style takes multiplied by the hourly pay you want.
**Add them together** to get your minimum price. Then compare with what good stylists near you charge, and round to a clear figure.

blocks.title: What a price must cover
items: Profit for growth
Your time (hourly pay)
Overhead share
Materials
blocks.caption: Build the price from the bottom up; the top layer is what lets your business grow.

blocks.title: Worked example: pricing medium knotless braids
blocks.context: For example, Bisi in Lagos wants to price medium knotless braids, mid-back length, with the client bringing her own extension hair. All figures are approximate.
steps: Materials (gel, mousse, bands, hot water): about 800 naira.
Overheads: about 15,000 naira a month for disinfectant, washing, data, transport and tools, across about 25 clients = 600 naira per client.
Time: 5 hours. She wants to earn at least 3,000 naira an hour, so 5 x 3,000 = 15,000 naira.
Minimum price: 800 + 600 + 15,000 = 16,400 naira.
Good braiders in her area charge about 18,000 to 25,000 naira for this style. She sets 20,000 naira, which leaves about 3,600 naira for growth.
If the client wants Bisi to supply the hair, she adds the cost of the packs at the price she paid, plus a little for her time buying them.
blocks.result: Bisi's price of 20,000 naira covers all her costs and her time, fits her local market, and leaves money to save for better tools.

blocks.title: Prices vary a lot
blocks.text: All naira figures in this course are approximate examples. Prices differ between cities, between areas of the same city, and over time as costs change. Check five or more local stylists, salon price lists or WhatsApp catalogues near you before setting yours, and review your prices every few months.
A clear price list
Presenting your service on WhatsApp

**WhatsApp Business** is a free app that lets you set up a business profile with your address, opening hours and a catalogue of services with photos and prices. Use quick replies for common questions, such as price, how long a style takes, and whether hair is included. Post one portfolio photo with a short caption on your status a few times a week, rather than ten photos at once.

items: **Say what makes your work different** in one sentence, for example: "Neat, gentle braids with clean tools for every client."
**Show proof**: a before and after, a day-7 photo, a short client comment shared with permission.
**Make booking easy**: state the price, the deposit if any, your account details for transfer, and your location.
**Be clear about your rules**: lateness, cancellations and what is included.

blocks.text: Taking payment smoothly

Most clients now pay by bank transfer. Put your account name, number and bank on your WhatsApp profile or catalogue so clients do not need to ask. A POS terminal or business account from providers such as Moniepoint or Opay can help if many clients want to pay by card, but compare the charges first. Always give the client a simple receipt or confirmation message, and record the payment in your log the same day.

blocks.title: Deposits protect your time
blocks.text: For long styles, many braiders ask for a small deposit to hold the booking. State it clearly, confirm it arrives in your own banking app, and deduct it from the final price.

When a client says your price is too high, do not argue or drop it immediately. Explain what is included, such as clean tools, a careful scalp check and a comfortable finish, and offer a cheaper option instead, such as bigger braids or shorter length, which take less time.

takeaways: Price = materials + overhead share + your time, then check the local market
Know your minimum price and do not go below it
A clear price list states what is included and how long it takes
Use WhatsApp Business: profile, catalogue, quick replies, regular status posts
Offer a smaller option instead of cutting your price

activity.title: Build your price list
steps: Choose four services you can do well.
Calculate materials, overhead share and time for each, and work out your minimum price.
Check at least five local stylists' prices for the same services.
Write your final price list and add it to a WhatsApp Business catalogue or a single image.
activity.evidence: Your pricing calculation for four services, the five local price comparisons, and a screenshot of your price list or catalogue.

lessons.title: Certification checklist and your 90-day plan
objectives: Check your capstone evidence against the certification requirements
Write an honest reflection on feedback and improvement
Set 90-day targets for clients, skills and income
Choose a next learning step after this course

blocks.text: You have learned how afro-textured hair behaves, how to wash and moisturise it, how to keep tools clean, how to braid cornrows, twists and box braids safely, how to handle chemical services responsibly, and how to price and track your work. This last lesson pulls it together into your certificate submission and a plan for the next three months.

blocks.name: certification
blocks.caption: Your certificate is earned by real evidence of safe, quality work, plus the final quiz.

blocks.text: Certification requirements

To qualify for the WODDI Institute certificate, you must complete the practical capstone and score at least 70 percent in the final quiz. The app will ask you to confirm the practical work is complete before you submit the quiz. Be honest: the evidence is for your own growth as much as for the certificate.

blocks.title: Capstone evidence pack
items: Five documented styles
Wash-day before and after
Hygiene station photo
Safety and consent card
Price list and log
Reflection and 90-day plan
blocks.caption: Tick each item off before you take the final quiz.

blocks.text: Writing your reflection
A good reflection is short and specific. Answer four questions in five to eight sentences:

items: What could I not do at the start that I can do now?
What specific feedback did I receive (from clients, volunteers or a mentor)?
What did I change because of that feedback, and what happened?
What is still my weakest point, and how will I improve it?

blocks.text: Your 90-day plan

Ninety days is long enough to build habits and a small client base, and short enough to stay focused. Split it into three 30-day blocks with one main aim each, and measure using the service log you started in Module 3.

head: Period
Main aim
Example targets
rows: Practise one weak skill 30 minutes daily; 8 clients; set up WhatsApp Business catalogue; post 3 photos a week
15 clients; repeat rate of at least 30 percent; collect 5 day-7 photos; review prices
20 clients; add one new style; save a fixed amount weekly for tools; write a monthly report each month

blocks.title: Worked example: setting realistic targets
blocks.context: For example, Hauwa in Abuja can braid on Fridays after 3 p.m. and all day Saturday. She currently does about 3 clients a month for friends.
steps: She has about 14 working hours a week, or about 56 hours a month.
Her average style takes 3 hours including clean-up, so she could do up to about 18 clients a month if fully booked.
She sets 8 clients for month 1, 12 for month 2 and 15 for month 3, leaving time for practice and rest.
At an average profit of about 7,000 naira per client (approximate), month 3 would bring about 15 x 7,000 = 105,000 naira profit.
She plans to save 10 percent of profit for a mannequin head and better scissors.
blocks.result: Hauwa's targets fit the hours she really has, grow step by step, and are measured in her service log, so she will know at day 90 whether the plan worked.

blocks.text: Next steps after this course

items: Work alongside an experienced stylist for some weeks to build speed and learn advanced styles, especially before offering chemical services.
Look for a recognised vocational or trade training programme in cosmetology or hairdressing in your state for a formal qualification.
If you plan to make and sell your own hair products, learn about NAFDAC registration first, and register your business name with the CAC when you are ready to grow.

blocks.text: If you fall behind your targets at day 30 or day 60, do not abandon the plan. Look at your log and find the reason: too few enquiries, enquiries that did not book, or clients who did not return. Each has a different fix: more visible posts, clearer prices and booking details, or better aftercare and follow-up messages. Change one thing and measure again.

blocks.title: Keep the standards you learned
blocks.text: As you get busy, it is tempting to skip hygiene or rush tension at the hairline. Keep the rules: clean and disinfect tools after every client, no styling over infection, no painful braids, and no chemical service without a scalp check, strand test and consent.

Remember why the numbers matter. Targets are not there to make you feel guilty; they show you what is working. A month with fewer clients but a higher repeat rate and no comfort complaints may be a stronger month than a busy one full of rushed work.

Share your 90-day plan with one person who will check in with you, such as a WODDI mentor, a friend or a family member. Meet or message them at day 30, 60 and 90 with your numbers from the log, and adjust the next block based on what you learned.

takeaways: Certificate: complete capstone evidence and at least 70 percent in the final quiz
Reflections are specific: feedback received, change made, result
Plan 90 days in three blocks, with targets that fit your real hours
Measure progress with your service log
Keep hygiene and safety standards as you grow

activity.title: Assemble and submit
steps: Gather every item on the capstone checklist into one folder or album.
Write your reflection using the four questions.
Write your 90-day plan with targets for each 30-day block.
Share the plan with one accountability partner and set check-in dates.
Confirm the practical task in the app and take the final quiz.
activity.evidence: Your complete evidence pack, reflection, and 90-day plan with check-in dates.

quiz.q: Which photo best shows a new client that your braids are gentle and long-lasting?
options: A day-7 photo showing neat braids and a calm hairline
quiz.explain: A real photo a week later shows the style holds and the edges are not irritated.

quiz.q: A client agrees to portfolio photos but asks that her face is not shown. What should you do?
options: Use back and side views only and note her choice on the client card
Post her face anyway since she agreed to photos
quiz.explain: Consent has limits. Respect them and record them so you do not make a mistake later.

quiz.q: Materials cost 500 naira, overhead share is 700 naira, and a style takes 3 hours at a target pay of 2,500 naira per hour. What is the minimum price?
quiz.explain: 3 x 2,500 = 7,500, plus 500 and 700 = 8,700 naira minimum.

quiz.q: A client says your knotless braid price is too high. What is the best response?
options: Argue that other salons are worse
Explain what is included and offer bigger or shorter braids at a lower price
quiz.explain: Offering a smaller option keeps your hourly pay fair while still meeting her budget.

quiz.q: What score do you need in the final quiz, along with the capstone, to earn the certificate?
quiz.explain: The rule is completing the practical capstone and scoring at least 70 percent in the final quiz.

quiz.q: Hauwa has 56 working hours a month and each style takes about 3.5 hours including clean-up. About how many clients can she serve at most?
quiz.explain: 56 divided by 3.5 is 16, so about 16 clients is her maximum if fully booked.

finalQuiz.q: Why do the ends of 4C hair often feel dry even when the scalp is oily?
options: The hair is low porosity everywhere
Sebum struggles to travel down tightly coiled strands
Shampoo removes moisture only from the ends
finalQuiz.explain: Scalp oil cannot move easily past the many bends of coily hair, so the ends need moisture from outside.

finalQuiz.q: A client finds a ball of hair after taking down six-week braids. Most strands have a small white bulb at one end. What does this show?
options: Normal shed hair that was trapped in the braids
finalQuiz.explain: Hairs with a bulb are shed hairs. They build up inside braids over the weeks and come out at takedown.

finalQuiz.q: Which order matches the LCO method?
finalQuiz.explain: LCO is liquid or leave-in first, then cream, then oil to seal. LOC puts oil before cream.

finalQuiz.q: What is the correct order for hygiene after each client?
options: Remove hair, wash with soap, rinse, soak for label time, dry and store covered
Wipe with a towel and reuse
finalQuiz.explain: Cleaning comes first because disinfectant cannot work through hair and product. Then soak for the full label contact time.

finalQuiz.q: Before starting braids, which consultation answer should make you stop and reconsider the service?
options: She wants to pay by transfer
She relaxed her hair three days ago and part of her scalp is sore
She plans to keep the style for five weeks
finalQuiz.explain: A sore scalp after a recent relaxer may be a chemical burn; tension and products could make it worse.

finalQuiz.q: In an underhand cornrow, why does the braid sit raised on the scalp?
options: Because you do not add hair along the row
Because the outer strands cross under the middle strand
finalQuiz.explain: Crossing the outer strands under the middle pushes the braid up on top of the scalp, the classic cornrow look.

finalQuiz.q: A client's new cornrows show small bumps and tenting at the temples. What is the right action?
options: Loosen or redo those rows with lighter tension
Tell her it will loosen in a few days
Apply heavy grease to the bumps
finalQuiz.explain: Bumps and tenting signal too much tension, which can lead to traction alopecia. Fix it before she leaves.

finalQuiz.q: During a relaxer retouch, where should the relaxer be applied?
options: On all the hair from root to tip
Only on the untreated new growth
finalQuiz.explain: Overlapping onto previously relaxed hair over-processes it and causes breakage.

finalQuiz.q: Relaxer splashes into a client's eye. What should you do first?
options: Wipe it with a dry towel
Apply neutralising shampoo to the eye
Rinse with plenty of clean running water for at least 15 minutes and get medical help
Wait to see if it hurts
finalQuiz.explain: Immediate, prolonged rinsing with water is the first aid for alkali in the eye, followed by medical help.

finalQuiz.q: Cornrows sell for 5,000 naira, use 300 naira of materials and take 1.5 hours. Twists sell for 7,000 naira, use 1,000 naira and take 3 hours. Which earns more per hour?
options: Twists, because the price is higher
Twists, at about 3,000 naira per hour
Cornrows, at about 3,130 naira per hour
finalQuiz.explain: Cornrows: 4,700 / 1.5 = about 3,130 per hour. Twists: 6,000 / 3 = 2,000 per hour.

finalQuiz.q: A client agrees to photos but not to her face being shown. Where should you record this?
options: On her client card, with the date
finalQuiz.explain: Recording consent on the client card protects her privacy and helps you avoid mistakes later.

finalQuiz.q: Materials are 800 naira, overhead share 600 naira, and the style takes 4 hours at 3,000 naira per hour. What is the minimum price?
finalQuiz.explain: 4 x 3,000 = 12,000, plus 800 and 600 = 13,400 naira minimum before comparing with local prices.

capstone.title: Hair care and styling portfolio with service records
capstone.brief: Complete and document five styles on at least three real people plus one full wash-day service, supported by client cards, finish-check scores, a hygiene station photo, a chemical safety and consent card, a priced service list, a service log, a reflection on feedback, and a 90-day plan.
steps: Set up your hygiene station and safety and consent card, and photograph them.

Complete one full wash day with LOC or LCO, with before and after photos.

Score each style with the six-point finish check and collect a comfort rating and a day-7 photo where possible.
Build a priced service list from your real costs and five local price comparisons, and keep a service log.
Write a reflection on feedback and a 90-day plan with targets for each 30-day block.
